By [Mara Okonkwo](https://example.test/staff/mara-okonkwo)

12 November 2026

Seagrass meadows in the inner harbour have spread across almost twice the area recorded five years ago, according to a survey published on Wednesday by the regional water authority.

Divers mapped forty-one hectares of eelgrass between the breakwater and the old ferry terminal this summer, up from twenty-two hectares in the previous survey. The authority credits the recovery to a ban on anchoring in the shallows and to the closure of two storm-water outfalls that once carried silt into the bay.

"We expected the meadows to hold their ground, not to double," said Dr Ines Valdivia, the marine ecologist who led the dive teams. "Seagrass is usually slow to come back once it has gone, so this is a genuinely encouraging result for the whole estuary."

## What changed

The anchoring ban came into force in 2022 after local sailing clubs agreed to move their moorings to fixed buoys further out. Volunteers have since replanted about three hectares by hand, tying shoots to biodegradable hessian mats and sinking them at low tide.

The full findings, including maps for each survey block, are set out in [the authority's report](https://example.test/reports/harbour-survey-2026.pdf). The next survey is planned for the summer of 2028.

Fishing groups welcomed the news, noting that juvenile snapper and flounder shelter in the meadows. Some boat owners, however, say the buoy fees are too high and have asked the council to review them before the next season begins.
